There are three routes to meditation on Koh Samui. Dipabhavan, the Samui branch of the Suan Mokkh forest monastery in the hills above Lamai, runs silent multi-day courses on a donation basis, with simple vegetarian meals and shared rooms. The Samui International Meditation Center in Bophut offers monk-led retreats (7 nights in a private forest bungalow for about US$405 with two meals a day), and wellness resorts such as Kamalaya, Absolute Sanctuary and Vikasa include meditation in their programmes. On the mainland, Suan Mokkh's international hermitage near Chaiya holds a 10-day silent retreat from the 1st to the 11th of every month for 2,000 THB, with in-person registration only.

Temple silent retreats: Dipabhavan

Dipabhavan Meditation Center sits in the forested hills of Maret, inland from Lamai (GPS 9.4605, 100.0257). It is a branch of Suan Mokkh, the forest monastery founded by the Thai teacher Buddhadasa Bhikkhu, and teaches mindfulness of breathing (anapanasati) in the same tradition. Courses are silent and residential, with a full daily timetable of guided sitting, walking meditation, readings and stretching. Accommodation is basic and shared, with mattresses, pillows and mosquito nets, and meals are simple and vegetarian.

  • Cost: donation-based; bed and meals are included.
  • Language: most courses are taught in Thai; English-language retreats are scheduled through the year, so check the centre's calendar before you plan around one.
  • Registration: through the centre's own activity portal, well in advance.
  • Season: January to September is the comfortable time; October to December is the rainy season, when the hill roads are slippery.

Dipabhavan on Google Maps. The road up is steep and narrow: take a taxi rather than a scooter, especially after rain.

Monk-led retreats in Bophut

The Samui International Meditation Center at 106/23 Moo 1, Bophut, in the north-east of the island and under 15 minutes from the airport, runs residential retreats taught by resident Buddhist monks using the Middle Way method. A typical 7-night programme includes daily meditation classes, Buddhist teachings, two meals a day, a private forest bungalow and an airport transfer, priced at about US$405 in 2026. Participants are asked to stay on site for the retreat, put devices aside and wear loose, modest clothing (no sleeveless, short or see-through clothes).

Meditation at resorts and yoga retreats

For a gentler introduction alongside comfort, Samui's wellness resorts include guided meditation, breathwork and mindfulness in their programmes. Kamalaya at Laem Set runs daily holistic activities and spiritual sessions within its wellness programmes; Absolute Sanctuary near Choeng Mon offers a Yoga Immersion and Mindfulness programme; and Vikasa on the cliffs near Coral Cove includes meditation and pranayama in its retreats and runs a set-date silent retreat. These are far more expensive than temple retreats but offer private rooms, spa treatments and flexible dates. Compare them in our wellness resorts guide and on the yoga page.

Mainland retreat nearby: Suan Mokkh

The Suan Mokkh International Dharma Hermitage, near Chaiya on the mainland north of Surat Thani, runs one of Thailand's best-known retreats for foreigners: 10 days of silent meditation from the 1st to the 11th of every month. Allow most of a day to get there from Samui by ferry and road.

  • Cost: 2,000 THB, non-refundable, covering everything for the 10 days.
  • Registration: in person only, on the last day of the previous month, 07:00–15:00, first come, first served. No advance booking by email or phone.
  • Rules: full silence; phones, tablets and notebooks are handed in; no joining late or leaving early.
  • Daily life: two vegetarian meals a day plus an evening drink; a small private room with shared bathrooms.
  • Dress: shoulders to below the knees covered, including upper arms; no see-through clothing.
  • Health: the retreat is not suitable for people with mental-health conditions or addictions; you must be in good physical and mental health.

Arriving a day early gets you a free night at the main monastery. Book your Samui departure and ferry so you arrive on the morning of registration day at the latest; see Surat Thani to Koh Samui for boats and buses in the other direction.

A typical day on a silent retreat

Timetables vary by centre; this is the general shape of a day at a temple-style silent retreat in the Suan Mokkh tradition.

  1. 04:00 Wake-up bell; morning reading and sitting meditation.
  2. 05:30 Yoga or stretching.
  3. 07:00 Breakfast in silence, followed by chores such as sweeping.
  4. 09:00 Dhamma talk, then alternating sitting and walking meditation.
  5. 12:00 Main meal of the day.
  6. 14:00 Sitting and walking practice, sometimes a question time with a teacher.
  7. 18:00 Evening drink and chanting.
  8. 19:30 Final sitting; lights out around 21:00.

How to prepare

  • Practise at home: sit for 20–30 minutes a day for a couple of weeks before you go; the long sittings are the hardest part.
  • Cut down on caffeine in the week before, as temple retreats rarely serve coffee.
  • Arrive rested: don't go straight from an overnight flight or a Full Moon Party into a silent retreat.
  • Bring: modest light clothes, a shawl, slippers, a torch, insect repellent, a water bottle, earplugs and any medication you need.
  • Tell someone where you'll be and when you'll be reachable again.

What to expect, and the rules

  • Silence: on silent retreats, no talking, gestures or eye contact with other participants; questions go to teachers at set times.
  • Early starts: temple schedules often begin around 04:00–05:00 with a wake-up bell, and end after an evening sitting.
  • Phones: handed in or switched off for the duration. Sort visas, flights and money before you start.
  • Food: vegetarian, often two meals a day with nothing solid after noon. Special diets are rarely possible at temple retreats.
  • Dress: loose, modest, light-coloured clothes covering shoulders and knees; no tight or revealing clothing.
  • Precepts: retreats ask you to keep the Buddhist precepts: no killing (including insects), stealing, sexual activity, lying, alcohol or drugs.
  • Leaving: you can leave a temple retreat if you need to, but tell the staff, and don't expect your donation or fee back.

Etiquette with monks

  • Women must not touch a monk or hand anything to him directly; place it on a cloth or table, or give it to a man to pass on.
  • Sit lower than monks where possible, with your feet tucked behind you and never pointing at a monk or a Buddha image.
  • Greet with a wai (palms together at the chest, a slight bow).
  • Remove shoes before entering halls and living quarters.
  • Ask before photographing monks, and don't use flash in halls.
  • Buddhist holy days bring a ban on alcohol sales in shops; licensed venues and hotels may still serve.

For temple visits generally, see our temples guide and Thai culture and traditions; Wat Khunaram, where the body of the meditation teacher Luang Pho Daeng sits in a glass case, is covered in its own guide.

After the retreat: easing back

Many people find the first day after a silent retreat overwhelming: traffic, music and conversation feel loud. Plan a quiet first night, eat simply, and keep the first day free of travel if you can. Keep a short daily sitting going for a few weeks to hold on to what you learned.

Best season for a meditation retreat

PeriodConditions
January–AprilDry and sunny; comfortable nights in the hills; the busiest time at retreats
May–SeptemberHot (highs 32–33 °C) with short showers; quieter
October–DecemberRainy season, wettest in November; slippery hill roads and more mosquitoes

Bring insect repellent all year: forest retreats are in mosquito country and dengue is present on Samui.

Combine meditation with yoga, spa and the sea

After a silent retreat, ease back gently. A Thai massage at a good shop (about 300–500 THB an hour) or a session in the herbal steam caves at Tamarind Springs (1,500 THB++) is a good first afternoon; see the spa guide. For quiet time on the water, the Pig Island sunset tour (1,550 THB, 5–6 hours with dinner) runs every day of the year, and from 16 December the boutique yachting day takes you to Ang Thong Marine Park on a wooden gulet (4,500 THB, park fee included). The shorter Pig Island speedboat is a half day. For an overview of every programme, see the retreats hub.
